messages.body_plain:
Cybil,

Please read the help files for the functions more carefully.

First, for readland.tps:

“Landmark coordinates are multiplied by their scale factor if this is provided for all specimens.”

This means as they are read in the scale is taken into account in the coordinates.

Second, for writeland.tps

“scale    An optional vector containing the length of the scale for each specimen”

This is not a T/F option, but a vector of numbers. However, in your case it is completely unnecessary as the scale was already incorporated in the landmark data when read into geomorph.

Dean

Whether R reads in loc as a factor or not is not particularly relevant here, but in any case if you want it to be a factor you can do something like classifier$loc <- as.factor(classifier$loc).

But maybe I am not understanding you correctly. At any rate, this sounds more like a basic R issue than a geomorph one, so maybe you should consider building some more general R knowledge? Plenty of online resources exist for that.

All the best,

Antigoni

messages.subject: Help with plotreftotarget
messages.subject_clean: Help with plotreftotarget
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I am working with different populations of snails which appear to have different morphologies. I have been using the plotreftotarget function to compare the deformations of the minimum / maximum of principal components 1 and 2 to understand where on my snails the difference in shape is mostly occurring.
I have two questions:
1) I would like to generate populations specfic deformation grids (I have read advice from previous discussions to no success, cannot subset properly?)
2) I would like to use the populations' specific deformations grids on a CVA plot (attached) to demonstrate which populations have what general morphology.

Cheers,
Angus
messages.body_snippet: Hello everyone, I am working with different populations of snails which appear to have different morphologies. I have been using the plotreftotarget function to compare the deformations of the minimum

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with plotreftotarget
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Help with plotreftotarget
messages.body_plain:
Angus,

1) For that you just need general R-indexing to filter each population, and then from that you can calculate the mean shape of each population and make deformation grids to compare them (with each other, or to the grand mean), e.g.

sh.pop1 <- shape[,,pop=="pop1"]

mean.pop1 <- mshape(sh.pop1)

grand.mean <- mshape(shape)

plotRefToTarget(grand.mean, mean.pop1)

This assumes you have a grouping object called pop, and (superimposed) shape data in a 3d-array called "shape"

2) If your objective is to review the shapes of each group, the approach above should be enough. For numerous reasons, I would recommend a PCA over a CVA plot for examining where these groups lie in morphospace and how much they overlap. For a detailed account on why this is the case, please read:

Klingenberg, C. P., and L. R. Monteiro. 2005. Distances and directions in multidimensional shape spaces: implications for morphometric applications. Syst. Biol. 54:678–688.

Mitteroecker, P., and F. L. Bookstein. 2011. Linear Discrimination, Ordination, and the Visualization of Selection Gradients in Modern Morphometrics. Evol. Biol. 38:100–114.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.subject: New R package, RRPP (0.3.0) available on CRAN
messages.subject_clean: New R package, RRPP (0.3.0) available on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

As a bit of follow-up to Dean’s announcement about the geomorph update, I wish to alert you to another R package we recently released (and have updated a little), RRPP, found on CRAN or at my Github site, https://github.com/mlcollyer/RRPP.

Those of you familiar with the analytical/statistical functions of geomorph will recognize the use of randomizing residuals in a permutation procedure (RRPP) as a means for generating empirical sampling distributions for e.g., ANOVA statistics or statistics for pairwise comparisons.  However, RRPP is a package intended for analysis of high-dimensional data of any sort (not just shape data), with a framework that resembles R’s lm function (for linear models), plus S3 generic functions, including coef, predict, plot, and anova.  Some of the features of this package include:
Types I, II, or III sums of squares and cross-products estimation
Effect size estimation (as z-scores) from SS, MS, Rsq, F, of Cohen’s f-squared distributions
Generalized least-squares (GLS) estimation, in addition to ordinary LS (OLS) estimation
Either continuous data matrices or distance matrices can be analyzed
Pairwise tests of means, slopes, or variances
Prediction and classification options
We introduce the package here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13029; and also provide a tutorial vignette with the package.  (Please note that some new functions have been added since the article was published.)  In the article we also demonstrate that the package is quite computationally proficient, especially compared to some similar packages.

The linear model function, lm.rrpp, produces output arranged hierarchically to include linear model (LM) statistics and ANOVA statistics, over many (user-defined) permutations.  Additionally, all permutation information (sampling frames, seed, and method) is saved, permitting a multitude of downstream, package- or user-defined analyses.  We believe the RRPP package format should facilitate ingenuity for advanced R users, while retaining a simple and clear format for typical linear model analyses, for novices and advanced users, alike.  Finally, although the package is geared toward high-dimensional data analysis, the functions work well with data of any dimension.

Please note that starting with version 3.0.7, geomorph now uses some RRPP functions as dependencies.  For those of you who like to download geomorph from Github, it will be wise to also update RRPP from Github when updating geomorph.

Cheers!

Mike Collyer and Dean Adams

messages.body_plain:
Sam, and everyone,

I would not get caught thinking about modularity and integration as two ends of the same continuum. Modularity implies greater covariation of variables within modules than between them. Integration means that two modules (matrices) are more correlated than you would expect from chance by random assortment of pairs of observations from each module. These are different definitions, statistically. The method of resampling is different between them.

No reason to expect contrasting results.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Sam,

As I was composing this Mike sent a very succinct and correct response. For completeness I’ll send my verbose version; though Mike’s hits the issue perfectly!

Dean

----

No this is not a mistake. It is possible to have both integration between modules and modularity within them. The problem is that many have thought of these as opposite ends of a continuum, which they are not. This false spectrum from modularity à integration is unfortunately perpetuated from prior researchers using the RV coefficient for both.  The logic was that since both modularity and integration could be ‘measured’ using RV, and since low RV = modular and high RV = integration, then data must display one or the other pattern. That is not entirely correct (for modularity it could be under some circumstances, but definitely not for integration among modules).   My 2016 MEE paper discusses this issue, as well as problems with the RV coefficient.

The issue here, as Mike mentioned, is in the null hypotheses tested and how they are evaluated. Modularity asks whether the observed modules are display more within-group covariation relative to between-group covariation. That is tested by creating ‘random’ modules and comparing the observed modularity measure to these (more formally, permute the columns of the data matrix, such that new modules are produced).

Integration via PLS asks whether the observed covariation between modules is greater than expected by chance. This is evaluated by permuting the ROWS of one module relative to the other. Note that for this hypothesis, no mention of covariation within-modules is dealt with; either mathematically or even biologically.

Now the thought experiment.  If one is investigating integration via PLS, by definition that is a question of integration among modules. But how can one have integration within modules without those modules displaying modularity?  One cannot.

This is why one can have both modularity and integration in the same dataset. Modularity states that there are sets of variables that are inter-correlated. Integration states that these sets of variables are more correlated with each other than one might expect.

Dean
